title: Plugin and modular architecture
idea: A pluggable, modular architecture splits a system into a stable core and independent plugins that the core discovers, starts and isolates through one published contract.
points: A plugin is a separate unit the host finds and starts at run time.
Plugins reach the host only through a small host API, never its internals.
Config, not code, decides which plugins are on; the core is not recompiled.
Unlike one extension point, plugins have a lifecycle, and the host contains their throws.

steps.caption: The host starts and reads which plugin ids are enabled. It knows plugins only by id.
`csv` is known, so the host creates it and calls `start`, passing only the narrow `HostApi`.
`CsvExport` registers an `export` command through the API. It never touches the host's fields.
`Broken` throws inside `start`. The host catches it, turns it off and keeps loading.
Nothing is installed for `pdf`, so the host skips that id instead of crashing.
A user runs `export`. The host routes it to whichever plugin registered that command.
Later, a PDF plugin ships as its own jar. The config already names `pdf`, so the host loads it without any code edit.

code.title: A tiny plugin host
code.caption: The host loads plugins by id from a config list. A missing or failing plugin does not stop it.

walk.text: Two contracts: what a plugin implements, and the small API the host offers back.
A registry maps ids to factories; in production, discovery fills it.
An enabled id with no installed plugin is skipped, not fatal.
A plugin that throws in `start` is turned off; the others still load.
Commands route by name, so the host never names a plugin class.
Plugins are typed against `HostApi` only; a host can pass an adapter so a cast cannot reach `Host`.

code.title: Real discovery with modules
code.caption: With the Java module system, each plugin jar declares what it provides, and `ServiceLoader` finds it on the module path.

pitfalls: Do not let plugins import core internals; export only the contract package.
Catch plugin exceptions at the boundary; in-process plugins can still hang or exhaust memory.
Change the plugin contract rarely and additively; every plugin depends on it.

quiz.q: After this load, what does `host.run("export")` print?
options: Nothing: the host crashes on broken
quiz.why: The host catches the exception from `Broken.start` and moves on. `csv` still starts and registers `export`, so the command runs.

takeaway: A stable core, a narrow contract, and plugin failures caught at the boundary.

starters: How does ServiceLoader find plugins without the core naming them?
When is a plugin architecture overkill for a small service?
